 Tired of waiting, B.C. ditches daylight saving time while WA falls back
 Was outgoing Premier David Eby trying to flex on the US? Or did the province just get tired of waiting
 Oct. 29, 2026 9:00 a.m. 
 While Washingtonians will be changing clocks Halloween night in anticipation of daylight saving time ending, British Columbia won't change its clocks for the first time since announcing the province is keeping daylight saving time. ( Finn Wendt /Cascadia Daily News) 
 By 
 Annie Todd 
 Criminal Justice/Enterprise Reporter 
 No Q&A content found.
 On Sunday, British Columbia will stop turning back clocks while Washington state continues to play with time.
 The B.C. Legislative Assembly passed a law in 2019 that would allow for the province to make daylight saving time permanent. But for the past seven years, the government sat waiting for its American West Coast allies to get the message.
 Then came the announcement in March by outgoing B.C. Premier David Eby. Surrounded by elementary school-aged children dancing to “Celebrate” by the Black Eyed Peas, Eby said B.C. would pave the way in making daylight saving time permanent. 
 “The reality is they’re stuck, and we’re going to give them the push they need,” Eby said of the U.S. and its habitual clock adjustments.
 B.C. isn’t the only province keeping daylight saving time: Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario and the Northwest Territories will keep clocks the same come Sunday. Saskatchewan and Yukon already keep clocks the same through the year. 
 Eby didn’t go so far as to say his government’s decision to keep the clocks the same was because of how U.S. President Donald Trump has treated Canadian neighbors over the last two years. Trump has repeatedly said he desires making Canada the “51st State.” Then, trade negotiations between the two allies blew up this summer, leading to heavy tariffs on American and Canadian imports and exports.
 Rather, in a letter to Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek and California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Eby wrote he was making the decision on behalf of the well-being of British Columbians. But he still urged the leaders to push their Congressional delegations toward permanent daylight saving time.
 Linda Larson, a retired member of the Legislative Assembly, sponsored the daylight saving time bill, known as the Interpretation Amendment Act, in 2019. She told Cascadia Daily News she was surprised Eby announced the time change earlier this year since “it had been gathering dust.”
 Keeping daylight saving time was wildly popular in B.C. in 2018 when a government survey found 93% of British Columbians preferred it.
 Advertisement 
 Larson believes Eby might have been trying to distract people away from his own government’s missteps by taking a stand against America’s time-meddling. Eby, who called a snap election for B.C. in September, endured a stunning defeat on Oct. 24 , when the B.C. Conservative Party sailed to a historic win, the first time the party has won a majority since 1928.
 In the March news conference, after the elementary schoolers left, Eby spent more time answering questions about land titling and the budget than he did answering questions about time-change logistics. 
 “The reality is every once in a while our government will try to do something that is popular,” Eby said. “The goal is to hear British Columbians … We’re going to stand on our own two feet, we’re going to make decisions that are best for us, we’re going to look after our province.”
 At one point, Washington was ahead of its northern neighbor. The state Legislature passed a bill in 2019 (months before British Columbia did) to “hashtag ditch the switch,” said Sen. Marcus Riccelli, a Spokane Democrat who sponsored the legislation while he was still in the House of Representatives.
 Riccelli told CDN he brought the bill in part because of health and recreation, keeping people outside longer in the light. He noted in 2019 that Idaho and California expressed interest in joining Washington and B.C. by keeping daylight saving time.
 If Eby was making a political move on Canada’s part in keeping the clocks the same, Riccelli said “it would be a hilarious shot across the bow,” but he thinks daylight saving time is simply popular with the people.
 While B.C. didn’t need the permission of Prime Minister Mark Carney to “ditch the switch,” Washingtonians need the nod from the U.S. Congress and the president. For years, senators and representatives alike have tried and failed to make daylight saving time permanent.
 Even Trump expressed his support for keeping the clocks the same, writing in an Oct. 2 Truth Social post that Senate Republicans needed to “get moving on what I call the ‘No More Changing of Clocks Act,’” or the Sunshine Protection Act.
 The bill, which passed the House 308-117 in July, is currently sitting in a Senate committee and won’t likely be voted on until after the midterms — if it even gets a hearing.
 U.S. Sen. Patty Murray, left, and outgoing British Columbia Premier David Eby both support keeping daylight saving time for their respective constituencies. Eby made it happen; Murray is still waiting on her congressional colleagues. (Photo courtesy of Office of Patty Murray) 
 In a statement, longtime daylight saving time supporter and senior Democratic Washington state Sen. Patty Murray said she would keep pushing the bill through Congress.
 “People in Washington state deserve more sunshine when they’ll actually be able to enjoy it,” she said.
 For Riccelli, Congress passing permanent daylight saving time would be a sign government isn’t “a broken clock.”
 “Maybe if they see Congress can take action on something that’s wildly popular, they will have a little more faith and a little more interest in other policy interventions that can move our country forward,” he said.
 Whether it’s dubbed government ineptitude or a national sovereignty flex, British Columbians will get an extra hour of sweet daylight while Washingtonians will be stuck in the dark starting Sunday.
 Annie Todd is CDN’s criminal justice/enterprise reporter; reach her at annietodd@cascadiadaily.com ; 360-922-3090 ext. 130.
